start.responsibility: Entry-point task that initiates the design of an e-commerce microservice backend covering user auth, product catalog, order processing, payment, inventory, and notifications on a Java + Spring Cloud Alibaba stack.
start.implementation: Carried out as a planning/root task: it frames the overall architecture, enumerates the bounded contexts to be designed, and sequences the design activities before drilling into domain-specific detail (notably the order-processing deep dive).
start.design_intent: Exists as the top-level scope anchor so that downstream design nodes (and the eventual deliverable) remain aligned with a single coherent backend vision rather than fragmented per-service designs.
start.constraints: Must cover all six listed sub-domains (auth, catalog, orders, payment, inventory, notifications); must respect the Java + Spring Cloud Alibaba stack choice; must treat order processing as the most complex area requiring state-machine and distributed-transaction handling; output feeds a single downstream deliverable node.

deliverable.responsibility: Produces the final design deliverables for an ecommerce microservice system: a high-level architecture overview document and an in-depth order-processing design covering state machine, distributed transaction handling, sequence flows, and fault tolerance.
deliverable.implementation: Realized as a design-document deliverable (likely a README and supporting sections within docs/design/ecommerce-microservice) that consolidates architectural decisions and detailed sub-designs into written artifacts rather than running code.
deliverable.design_intent: Serves as the terminal artifact of the design exercise — a reviewer-facing, navigable record of the proposed system so stakeholders can validate both the macroscopic service topology and the microscopic correctness of the most complex flow (order processing) before implementation begins.
deliverable.constraints: Must remain at design-document scope (no production code), must be self-consistent across the overview and the order-processing detail, must explicitly address the four flagged concerns (state machine correctness, distributed transaction semantics, sequencing, fault tolerance), and must be traceable back to the upstream planning task that initiates the workflow.
